initial_presentation: A 13-year-old male patient was born to parents who are double first cousins, following an uncomplicated pregnancy and vaginal delivery. At the time of his conception, the father was 56 years old and the mother was 40 years old. There was a history of two neonatal deaths with unknown causes, two unaffected siblings, and two affected cousins. The patient exhibited early global developmental delay, progressive skeletal changes, and an abnormal gait starting at the age of two. He measured 115 cm in height (−5.6 SD) and had a head circumference of 48 cm (−4.16 SD). His weight was in the 10th percentile (36 kg), with a U/S ratio of 0.77 (normal ~0.9). Physical examination revealed coarse facial features, a low hairline, and prominent lips. He had a short trunk, short chest, broad elbow and wrist joints, and asymmetric genu valgum, more pronounced on the right side. His hands and feet were short and broad with brachydactyly of all fingers and toes, pes planus, prominent heels, and generalized hypertrichosis. An intellectual disability was noted with an IQ of 41. No abnormalities were observed in other body organs, and there were no visual or hearing impairments.

A 17-year-old male, who is right-hand dominant and previously healthy, arrived at the emergency department with pain, swelling, and numbness in his left hand. Three days earlier, he had injured his left hand while playing football, though he could not recall a specific incident such as a fall or tackle. He noticed pain and swelling in his hand after the game, which worsened over the next few days. Initial imaging at an outside hospital showed no fractures or dislocations. Despite this, his pain, paresthesia, and swelling, particularly in the thenar compartment, continued to worsen. On physical examination, there was significant tenderness and swelling in the left thenar eminence and thumb, without any overlying erythema or open wounds. The patient had a severely limited range of motion in the wrist and thumb joints due to severe pain and was unable to oppose his thumb. Passive thumb motion caused significant pain, and he reported decreased sensation on the radial side of his left thumb. Sensation, capillary refill, strength, and range of motion were normal in the other fingers. Repeat radiographs in the ED again showed no bony injuries. Despite the imaging results, the patient's clinical presentation included tense swelling of the left thenar compartment, pain, decreased range of motion, and sensory deficit. Compartment pressures in the thenar compartment of the left hand were measured using a Stryker needle, with readings of 72 and 73 mm Hg, and a diastolic blood pressure of 80 mm Hg. The patient was taken to the operating room for an emergent fasciotomy. Bloodwork prior to surgery revealed pancytopenia with profound neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, anemia, and leukopenia.

A 29-year-old male presented with a history of blurred vision 9 years ago. He underwent subtotal resection of a pineal region mass, and the pathology report indicated a specific type of pineal tumor. Within one month post-surgery, he developed acute hydrocephalus, necessitating the insertion of a ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt. Postoperatively, a stable residue of less than 2 cm was monitored for 2 years. A two-month-old male infant was born with a full Apgar score. He experienced neonatal jaundice that was managed with low-intensity phototherapy and was later discharged home. His mother observed noisy breathing starting from the second week of life, which intensified with activity. Additionally, the infant began having feeding difficulties. Upon admission and referral to the otorhinolaryngology team, physical examination revealed soft intermittent inspiratory stridor accompanied by subcostal and intercostal recession. Oxygen saturation was maintained at 100% with continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP).

The patient is a 13-year and 5-month-old boy with a congenital deformity of the left forearm. From the age of 3, his growth in height lagged behind peers, and his penis remained smaller than average for his age, with no development over the past two years. He was born with bilateral cryptorchidism and underwent bilateral orchidectomy. The patient has experienced reduced sweating since childhood, and his cognitive abilities are normal. He was delivered by caesarean section at term, with a birth weight of 3400 g and a birth length of 50 cm. He was fed artificially. His motor development was typical for his age and sex. The parents are not related by blood, and the mother had a healthy pregnancy. The father is 170 cm tall and healthy; the mother is 158 cm tall and has deformities in the distal segments of the little fingers of both hands, with no other health issues. The child's height, weight, and body mass index (BMI) are 144 cm (−2.4SD), 33.8 kg, and 16.3 kg/m2, respectively. The nipples are wide apart and retracted, the penis measures 2 cm × 1 cm, and the testicles have a volume of 1 ml. The 4th and 5th metacarpals and phalanges of the left hand are absent, as is the left ulna. The body is well-proportioned with no noticeable facial abnormalities or issues detected in the heart, lungs, or abdomen. Routine

Case 2 involves a 45-year-old architect with a history of childhood asthma. Throughout most of his adult life, his asthma has been well managed with minimal exacerbations and no hospital admissions. Recently, he has experienced a reduction in exercise tolerance and an increase in cough, producing purulent sputum with occasional thick or solid components. He has had several significant respiratory exacerbations that did not respond well to standard steroid and antibiotic treatments. During one severe episode, he required emergency hospital admission due to respiratory distress, which improved after expectorating very thick sputum. The patient is a 35-year-old married Chinese female (G3P0) who experienced elevated office blood pressure (approximately 159/96 mmHg) starting from the 16th week of gestation. The blood pressure continued to increase, reaching a maximum of approximately 180/110 mmHg, accompanied by palpebra and ankle edema. The hypertension was not managed with 30 mg nifedipine taken twice daily. At the 20th week of gestation, she was admitted to the Cardiovascular Department of West China Hospital, Sichuan University with hypertension. The patient had no personal or family history of hypertension, chronic kidney disease, diabetes mellitus, or autoimmune disease. Prior to gestation, she was healthy with no evident endocrine disorders. Upon admission at 20 weeks of gestation, her office blood pressure was 168/100 mmHg, weight was 68 kg, height was 162 cm, and body mass index was 25.9 kg/m2. Blood pressure readings were 168/100 mmHg in the left upper extremity, 166/98 mmHg in the right upper extremity, 180/110 mmHg in the left lower extremity, and 184/112 mmHg in the right lower extremity, with a normal upper to lower extremity blood pressure ratio. There were no signs of pulmonary edema, cerebral, or visual symptoms. Baseline serum glucose was 6.0 mmol/L and glycosylated hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) was 5.8%. Liver and renal functions were normal. No vascular murmurs were detected in the neck, chest, or abdomen. Hypertensive target organ damage was assessed, revealing a carotid femoral pulse wave velocity (cf-PWV) of 8.9 ± 0.8 m/s and a carotid intima media thickness (IMT) of 0.7 mm bilaterally with no atheromatous plaques. The urinary albumin/creatinine ratio (UACR) was 48.4 mg/g, and proteinuria was 0.43 g in a 24-hour urine collection.

An 11-year-old male presented with bilateral upper limb primary lymphedema characterized by significant swelling of the hands resembling 'boxing gloves.' Additional findings included lymphedema of the right thigh and genital area, along with widespread cutaneous lymph blisters, particularly on the trunk. Scattered red spider-like capillaries were also noted on the skin. There was no evidence of segmental overgrowth or venous issues.
